subChunks.title: Advanced TypeScript Patterns for React
subChunks.hookHtml: Basic TypeScript types catch typos. Advanced TypeScript patterns catch architectural mistakes. Discriminated unions, conditional types, template literal types, and utility types let you express complex component APIs in ways that make wrong usage impossible to compile. This lesson covers the patterns that senior React developers use to build truly type-safe component libraries.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Discriminated unions for variant components

// Instead of optional props that can be combined incorrectly:
type BadAlertProps = {
  type?: 'success' | 'error' | 'warning';
  onRetry?: () => void; // Only makes sense for 'error'
  onDismiss?: () => void;
};

// Discriminated union — invalid combinations are type errors:
type AlertProps =
  | { type: 'success'; message: string; onDismiss: () => void }
  | { type: 'error'; message: string; onRetry: () => void; onDismiss: () => void }
  | { type: 'warning'; message: string; onDismiss: () => void };

function Alert(props: AlertProps) {
  // TypeScript narrows the type based on props.type:
  if (props.type === 'error') {
    // TypeScript knows onRetry is available here
    return <div>{props.message} <button onClick={props.onRetry}>Retry</button></div>;
  }
  return <div>{props.message}</div>;
}

Polymorphic components — the `as` prop

// A Button that can render as any HTML element:
type ButtonProps<C extends React.ElementType = 'button'> = {
  as?: C;
  children: React.ReactNode;
  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary';
} & React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<C>;

function Button<C extends React.ElementType = 'button'>({
  as,
  children,
  variant = 'primary',
  ...rest
}: ButtonProps<C>) {
  const Component = as ?? 'button';
  return <Component className={`btn btn--${variant}`} {...rest}>{children}</Component>;
}

// Usage — TypeScript infers the correct prop set:
<Button>Click me</Button>            // button props
<Button as="a" href="/quests">Link</Button>  // anchor props
<Button as={Link} to="/quests">Link</Button> // React Router Link props

Utility types for component APIs

// Extract props from an existing component:
type ButtonProps = React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>;

// Extend native element props:
type InputProps = React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'input'> & {
  label: string;
  error?: string;
};

// Make some required fields optional:
type PartialQuestProps = Partial<QuestCardProps>;

// Pick specific fields:
type QuestSummary = Pick<Quest, 'id' | 'title' | 'xp'>;

// Exclude a type from a union:
type WithoutAdmin = Exclude<UserRole, 'admin'>;

Template literal types

// Type-safe CSS class variants:
type Size = 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg';
type Colour = 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'danger';
type ButtonClass = `btn-${Size}-${Colour}`;
// Valid: 'btn-sm-primary', 'btn-lg-danger' etc.
// Invalid: 'btn-xl-primary' — type error!

// Type-safe event handler prop names:
type EventName = 'click' | 'change' | 'submit';
type HandlerProps = {
  [K in EventName as `on${Capitalize<K>}`]?: () => void;
};
// Results in: { onClick?: () => void; onChange?: () => void; onSubmit?: () => void }

Conditional types

// A form field that is required or optional based on a generic:
type FieldProps<Required extends boolean = false> = {
  label: string;
  value: string;
} & (Required extends true
  ? { required: true; defaultValue?: never }
  : { required?: false; defaultValue?: string });

// Usage:
<Field<true> label="Email" value={email} required />  // must have required=true
<Field label="Bio" value={bio} defaultValue="" />       // optional, has defaultValue

Vex: "The goal of advanced TypeScript patterns is to make invalid states unrepresentable. If a component accepts onRetry only for error alerts — encode that in the type. If an as-prop Button accepts anchor-specific props when as='a' — encode that. Every invalid usage caught at compile time is a runtime error that never reaches a user."

storyBeats.text: A component that accepts 12 optional props — but only specific combinations are valid. Runtime errors when the wrong ones are combined. Vex opens the types file.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Advanced TypeScript doesn't just annotate values. It expresses the rules of your component API. A discriminated union makes invalid prop combinations a compile error. A polymorphic as prop gives the correct props for each element type. The type system becomes the documentation — and it's enforced.

storyBeats.speaker: Discriminated union preventing invalid prop combinations
storyBeats.text:
type ButtonProps =
  | { as: 'a'; href: string; onClick?: never }  // links use href
  | { as?: 'button'; href?: never; onClick: () => void }; // buttons use onClick

// TypeScript error — can't have both href and onClick:
<Button as="button" href="/quests" onClick={() => {}} />

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Apply advanced TypeScript patterns to a component API:

  • Build an Alert component using a discriminated union type. 'success' alerts have no onRetry; 'error' alerts require onRetry. Both have message and onDismiss.
  • Build an Input component that extends React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'input'> and adds a required label and optional error prop.
  • Define a Size and Colour union and a template literal type ButtonClass = \'btn-${Size}\''.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a fully typed polymorphic <Text> component that can render as any heading (h1-h6), paragraph, or span. The as prop determines the element and its allowed props. Add a size prop with values matching heading levels ('xs' | 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg' | 'xl' | '2xl') and a weight prop. Use conditional types to make htmlFor available only when as="label". Demonstrate that invalid usage produces compile errors.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain discriminated unions to a developer who uses optional props for variant components. What problem do they solve? Then explain the polymorphic `as` prop pattern — what TypeScript challenge does it solve and how does ComponentPropsWithoutRef help? Finally, explain when template literal types are useful.

questions.prompt: What is a discriminated union in TypeScript?
options: A union type where each variant has a common literal property (the discriminant) that TypeScript uses to narrow the type in conditional checks
A union type that excludes certain values
A type that discriminates between runtime and compile-time values
A union type defined with the `discriminate` keyword
questions.answer: A union type where each variant has a common literal property (the discriminant) that TypeScript uses to narrow the type in conditional checks
questions.explanation: A discriminated union has a shared property (the discriminant — like 'type') with a unique literal value in each variant. When you check props.type === 'error', TypeScript narrows the type to the error variant, making error-only properties available. This makes invalid prop combinations type errors — the type system encodes the component's rules.

options: The full TypeScript type of all valid HTML props for a button element, including onClick, disabled, type, etc. — without the ref prop
A generic type for any React component
The return type of a button component's render function
The props type excluding children and className
questions.answer: The full TypeScript type of all valid HTML props for a button element, including onClick, disabled, type, etc. — without the ref prop
questions.explanation: ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> extracts the props type from the built-in button element definition. Extending it for a custom Button component gives you all native button props plus your custom ones, and users get autocomplete for native props they already know. ComponentPropsWithRef includes the ref prop — needed when you forward refs.

questions.prompt: You have `type Size = 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg'` and `type Colour = 'red' | 'blue'`. What does `type ButtonClass = \'btn-${Size}-${Colour}\'` produce?
options: A string type that accepts any string starting with 'btn-'
An error — template literal types don't work with union types
questions.explanation: TypeScript distributes template literal types over union members. It generates all combinations of the constituent unions. This lets you write type-safe class name systems, event handler names, CSS variable names, or any string pattern where the valid values are a known set of combinations.

questions.prompt: A component has both an `href` prop (for anchor behaviour) and an `onClick` prop (for button behaviour). A developer passes both. Why is a discriminated union better than making both optional?
options: Optional props allow invalid combinations at compile time — both href and onClick can be passed together. A discriminated union makes only valid combinations possible.
Discriminated unions are faster at runtime
Optional props can't have different types; discriminated unions can
TypeScript requires discriminated unions for all components with more than 3 props
questions.answer: Optional props allow invalid combinations at compile time — both href and onClick can be passed together. A discriminated union makes only valid combinations possible.
questions.explanation: With optional props, <Button href="/quests" onClick={() => {}} /> compiles fine but behaves ambiguously. A discriminated union with { as: 'a'; href: string; onClick?: never } | { as?: 'button'; onClick: () => void; href?: never } makes it a type error to pass both. The type system enforces the contract at compile time, not at runtime with a console.warn.
